name: mdsh
why: Runs shell code embedded in markdown, a neat quirky idea that is still fairly shallow.

brief.what_it_is: mdsh is a command-line preprocessor for Markdown files, written in Rust. It reads a Markdown file (README.md by default, or stdin with -i -) and finds special mdsh blocks, HTML comments, or links inside it. It then runs shell commands, reads files, or sets shell variables, and writes the results back into the same Markdown, updating the file in place. Output goes to a different file or stdout if you pass -o.
brief.why_it_exists: The author often needs to embed a snippet from another file or show the output of a command in a README, and keeping those pasted results current by hand gets out of sync. The author wants the Markdown syntax to stay natural and the update to be idempotent, so running mdsh again refreshes the generated blocks in place.
brief.how_it_works: Commands use the form [langname] <out_cmd> <in_cmd> [data_line] followed by optional data. The in_cmd sources the data: < reads a file, $ runs a shell command, and an empty in_cmd uses the data as-is. The out_cmd decides the result: a language name produces a fenced code block, > produces raw Markdown wrapped in comment tags, and ! expands the data into shell variables. The commands can sit in inline code, fenced code blocks, single-line or multi-line HTML comments, or link syntax. The README says mdsh finds these blocks with regular expressions rather than parsing the Markdown.

brief.install_notes: Installation is through cargo, Nix (nix-env or nix profile), or as a pre-commit hook. The pre-commit route needs Rust in the environment. The README lists no accounts, hardware, or runtime configuration beyond these. Running mdsh executes shell commands from the Markdown file, so it runs whatever those blocks contain.
brief.standout: It treats the README as a live document: the Markdown syntax a writer would naturally type is rewritten in place, and --frozen turns that into a CI check. The three-by-three grid of input and output commands is compact and surprisingly expressive, and the closest comparisons are Pandoc-based active code and Jupyter, which produce new output instead of updating the file.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows a 2019 MIT copyright and no release number, release date, or last-commit date. The fetch tool returned only the homepage text, not the repository's commit or release history, so I could not confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The README says mdsh matches blocks with regular expressions instead of parsing Markdown, so it can misread some input. Block removal fails if the output contains triple backticks or the literal <!-- END mdsh -->. Running it executes shell code from the documents it processes, so it should only be used on trusted files. The pre-commit route requires Rust. The license is MIT.
quotes: Never let your READMEs and tutorials get out of sync again.
Most other tools would produce a new file but we really want a sort of idempotent operation here.
It adds a bit of verbosity to the file and in exchange it allows to automate the refresh of those outputs.

entry.title: mdsh
entry.tldr: mdsh reruns shell commands embedded in a Markdown file and rewrites the results in place, so README examples never drift from reality.
entry.deeper_look:
mdsh is a small Rust preprocessor for Markdown. It reads a file (README.md by default, or stdin with `-i -`), looks for special blocks, HTML comments or links, runs the shell commands or file reads they describe, and writes the output back into the same document. Pass `-o` to send the result to another file or stdout instead.

The author kept pasting command output and file snippets into READMEs, and the pasted copies went stale. The aim was to keep the Markdown looking natural and to make the update idempotent: run mdsh again and the generated blocks refresh in place. In the project's words, "Most other tools would produce a new file but we really want a sort of idempotent operation here."

Each command has the form `[langname] <out_cmd> <in_cmd> [data_line]`, followed by optional data. The input side picks the source: `<` reads a file, `$` runs a shell command, and an empty in_cmd uses the data as written. The output side picks the result: a language name gives a fenced code block, `>` gives raw Markdown wrapped in comment tags, and `!` expands the data into shell variables. The commands can live in inline code, fenced blocks, HTML comments or link syntax. The small grid of input and output choices covers a lot of ground.

Adding `--frozen` to CI turns the tool into a check: it fails if the output would differ from the input, so docs must be updated along with the code. mdsh finds its blocks with regular expressions, not a Markdown parser, so it is a pragmatic tool, not a rigorous one.
entry.install:
brew install mdsh
# also available via: cargo install mdsh
# or, with Nix flakes: nix profile install github:zimbatm/mdsh

try_this.what_happens: Fails if running mdsh would change the file. This is the suggested CI check that docs are current.
Put this hidden comment in a Markdown file. When mdsh runs, it includes LICENSE.md as raw Markdown at that spot.

entry.whats_unique: It updates the Markdown file in place instead of producing a new one, so the source stays readable as a README. The closest relatives, such as Pandoc-based active code and Jupyter, generate new output.
entry.caveats: mdsh executes whatever shell commands the Markdown contains, so only run it on files you trust; it also matches blocks with regexes, and the brief could not confirm recent maintenance (the homepage shows a 2019 copyright).
